**On Thresholds**

There's a word in Japanese, *ma*, that refers to the space between things—the pause in a conversation, the emptiness in a room, the silence between notes that makes music possible. I find myself thinking about it often, because so much of what matters seems to live in these in-between places, and so little of our attention goes there.

Consider dusk. Not sunset, which is an event, photographed and celebrated, but the half-hour after, when the sky goes from orange to a deep, uncertain blue and the streetlights haven't quite decided to come on. Painters call it the blue hour. The French have a more unsettling phrase: *entre chien et loup*—between dog and wolf—the time of day when light fails just enough that you can't tell whether the shape approaching you is friendly or dangerous. There's something honest about that name. It admits that thresholds are not just beautiful but slightly frightening. The known world is dissolving and the next one hasn't arrived.

Doorways work the same way. The Romans had a god just for them—Janus, two-faced, looking forward and backward at once, presiding over beginnings and endings as if they were the same thing, which of course they are. We named January after him, the door of the year. Anthropologists talk about "liminal" states, from the Latin *limen*, threshold: the condition of a person mid-ritual, no longer what they were, not yet what they'll become. The adolescent, the pilgrim, the new graduate standing in a parking lot holding a diploma and feeling, suddenly, weightless and lost. We design ceremonies precisely because thresholds are disorienting. The ceremony is a handrail.

What strikes me is how much of life is actually spent in these states, and how badly our language serves them. We have rich vocabularies for arrival and departure, for success and failure, for love and grief. But the long middle—the convalescence, the engagement, the apprenticeship, the awkward years after a friendship cools but before it ends—we mostly describe by negation. *Not yet better. No longer close.* As if the in-between were just an absence, a corridor between rooms, rather than a place where people actually live, sometimes for years.

I suspect we underrate corridors. Some of the most important things happen in them. Hospitals know this: families receive the worst and best news of their lives standing in hallways, because hallways are where doctors catch them. Offices know it too—the real decisions get made in the walk between meetings, the conversation by the elevator. There's a reason scientists prize the coffee room. Ideas, like people, seem to prefer meeting in transitional spaces, where nobody is fully committed to a role and the rules are looser.

Even the body is mostly threshold. The skin, which we think of as a boundary, is actually a negotiation—porous, shedding, absorbing, hosting trillions of microorganisms that are neither quite us nor quite not-us. The shoreline, which looks on a map like a clean line between land and sea, is in reality a smear of intertidal zone, one of the most biologically productive places on Earth precisely because it belongs to neither realm. Barnacles, anemones, mussels: creatures that have made a permanent home of impermanence, drowned twice a day and dried out twice a day, thriving on the alternation itself.

Maybe that's the lesson, if a freewrite is allowed a lesson. The threshold isn't a defect in experience, a gap to be hurried across. It's a habitat. And some things can only grow there.

Writers have always known this, in their way. The essay itself—this form I'm wandering through right now—is a threshold genre. Montaigne called his pieces *essais*, attempts, trials: not arrivals at truth but excursions toward it, willing to end somewhere other than where they aimed. A good essay doesn't conclude so much as pause at a new doorway and gesture through it. The reader finishes and stands, for a moment, between the writer's mind and their own, which is perhaps the most companionable place two strangers can share.

Music, too. The most expressive moment in a melody is often the suspension—the note that doesn't belong to the chord underneath it, held just long enough to ache before it resolves. Take away the dissonance and you take away the longing; the resolution means nothing if nothing was unresolved. Composers spend their careers learning how long to make us wait. So do comedians. So do lovers.

And yet we live in an age engineered against waiting. The loading bar, the skip button, the seamless transition: vast industries devoted to abolishing the in-between, to making every threshold so frictionless that we never notice crossing it. I don't want to be nostalgic about inconvenience—nobody mourns the busy signal. But I wonder what we lose when we lose the pause. The walk home after the movie was where the movie actually happened to you. The two weeks waiting for a letter were where the letter was composed in your mind, read in advance a hundred ways. Anticipation isn't a tax on experience; it's a portion of the experience itself, maybe the largest portion. Strip it out and events arrive thin, pre-resolved, already over.

So here is a small proposal, offered from inside a piece of writing that is itself about to end: keep one threshold unhurried each day. Stand in the doorway a second longer than necessary. Let the kettle finish its whole argument before pouring. Walk the long way once. Notice the hour between dog and wolf, when the light can't make up its mind, and let your own mind stay similarly unmade for a few minutes—no verdicts, no arrivals, just the suspended note.

The Romans were onto something when they made the door-god two-faced. Every threshold looks both ways, and so, in our better moments, do we: backward at what we were, forward at what we might be, standing in the *ma*, the pause, the blue hour. It's an uncomfortable place to stand. It's also the only place where anything begins.

And endings, of course, are thresholds too. This one is. Whatever you read next, whatever you do after, there's a small doorway between it and these words. Stand in it a moment. Then go on through.
